sections.heading: 1. Assign eighteen plays to five seats before adding capacity
paragraphs: Build one operating pod, not five loosely coordinated freelancers. For Candidate #28, the Conservative and Base configurations both contain two full-time seats and three contractor seats; an owner working daily must occupy a counted seat rather than become invisible labor. FT1 owns commercial performance, authorized-dealer relationships, purchasing economics, and the weekly close. FT2 owns order execution, inventory integrity, customer recovery, and the 3PL relationship. Contractor C1 delivers acquisition and creative production; C2 delivers retention and integration maintenance; C3 delivers bookkeeping and reconciliation. Contractors are bounded specialist capacity, not three additional full-time employees disguised by invoices. Record hours or deliverable capacity, replacement coverage, access scope, and acceptance criteria in each statement of work. At Scaled, add FT3 for customer experience and exception management, plus C4 for catalog and product-data quality. Transfer tasks explicitly instead of leaving the original employee accountable for everything. Shopify, Gorgias, Klaviyo, and the warehouse portal should each have a named internal owner and a documented recovery path. The outsourced warehouse remains a vendor organization outside the seven-person pod, but its fees and failures remain inside the economics. Use a shared exception queue so delegation changes visibility rather than concealing unfinished work.

Use the following eighteen-play operating map to make the assigned portfolio executable: P01 dealer authorization, P02 assortment underwriting, P03 landed-cost purchasing, P04 catalog publishing, P05 demand forecasting, P06 replenishment alerts, P07 order routing, P08 warehouse reconciliation, P09 delivery exceptions, P10 returns tracking, P11 refund control, P12 paid acquisition, P13 creative testing, P14 lifecycle retention, P15 cohort analysis, P16 accrual close, P17 product-safety evidence, and P18 transferability documentation. These labels are this chapter's working allocation of the eighteen mapped plays, not additional revenue streams. FT1 remains accountable for P01 through P03 and P12 through P18; FT2 remains accountable for P04 through P11, with specialist execution assigned in the seat matrix. C3 prepares accounting evidence but never releases its own vendor payments. C2 can repair a routing integration but cannot independently change payout destinations. Every play needs one primary owner, one trained backup, one measurable output, and one linked procedure. Rehearse absence coverage monthly by having the backup resolve a real exception from the documented queue. If the founder must interpret undocumented supplier promises or rescue every inventory mismatch, the pod has automated clicks rather than transferred operating knowledge. Correct that dependency before hiring another specialist to absorb its symptoms.

Buy contractor outcomes with retainers plus capped, auditable variable fees. An illustrative C1 agreement pays $1,200 monthly for eight accepted creative variants, campaign maintenance, and one contribution review; reserve any incentive for incremental contribution after media, refunds, and fulfillment, using a fixed baseline and attribution window. C2 might receive $900 monthly for monitored lifecycle flows and a bounded integration backlog; C3 might receive $600 for reconciliations and a documented monthly close. These example retainers total $32,400 annually before variable fees and are planning inputs, not additions to canonical profit. A critical routing incident requires acknowledgment within one covered business hour, a documented containment plan within four, and a next-business-day root-cause note. State coverage windows and emergency escalation separately; a small retainer does not purchase continuous staffing. Require written acceptance of creative rights, test orders, reconciliations, and change logs before paying disputed deliverables. Contracts do not determine worker classification by themselves: evaluate actual behavioral control, financial control, and the working relationship, plus applicable state tests. Preserve contractor discretion over methods where appropriate while retaining strict requirements for security and results. Budget employee payroll, taxes, benefits, and supervision explicitly before accepting the five-seat model as economically feasible.

sections.heading: 2. Run a weekly scorecard that exposes contribution and concentration
paragraphs: Hold a forty-five-minute weekly operating review using one frozen reporting cutoff, one metric dictionary, and links to underlying transactions. FT1 publishes net sales, contribution dollars, acquisition spend, cash availability, and supplier concentration; FT2 publishes routing success, overdue orders, available-to-promise accuracy, returns aging, and customer-contact backlog. C1 explains campaign economics, C2 explains lifecycle exceptions, and C3 reconciles material differences between commerce reports and the ledger. Define contribution consistently as recognized sales after refunds less product cost, outbound fulfillment, payment fees, variable return costs, and attributable advertising. Do not subtract a refund twice when the revenue number already excludes it. Separate contribution before advertising when diagnosing product economics, but label it explicitly. Revenue per person is secondary because warehouse labor is purchased externally and contractor capacity varies. Report contribution per internal operating hour alongside total outsourced spend. Each red metric must produce a named action, a deadline, and a quantified exposure, such as orders awaiting a carrier scan or dollars trapped in unreconciled returns. Close prior actions before discussing new experiments. The meeting succeeds when it changes an operating decision, not when every chart has an attractive trend. Archive the packet so a buyer can trace historical decisions.

Set initial service thresholds from the actual selling promise, then tighten them with evidence. A useful starting design targets at least 99.5% successful automated routing, at least 98% shipment within the promised window, and at least 99% agreement between sampled physical units and the inventory ledger. These are internal operating targets, not claims about existing performance. Define routing success as an eligible paid order acknowledged by the correct warehouse without manual repair; exclude documented fraud holds from both numerator and denominator. Track stockout exposure as forecast contribution lost, not merely the number of empty SKUs. For returns, report requests awaiting labels, parcels received but uninspected, refunds due, and resalable units awaiting restock separately. A warehouse receipt does not prove a refund was issued. Under 16 CFR 435.2, shipping promises need a reasonable basis, and qualifying delays require the prescribed customer options and refund handling. Configure alerts around those obligations rather than an arbitrary warehouse dashboard color. Test whether Shopify Flow or middleware retries create duplicate fulfillments and whether failed webhooks enter a visible dead-letter queue. Resolve root causes before rewarding contractors for increasing order volume through a visibly unstable fulfillment process.

Adopt a maximum 25% exposure policy for any single customer and each material commercial counterparty, with separate denominators rather than one misleading blended percentage. Measure customers by trailing twelve-month net sales, suppliers by trailing purchases, and warehouses by shipped orders; also track concentrated contribution and inventory replacement lead times. A consumer retailer may have negligible customer concentration while one distributor supplies most profitable products. Show both trailing twelve-month and latest-quarter views to catch rapid deterioration. One primary 3PL, processor, or storefront platform will often exceed the cap in a lean operation. Report that breach plainly; a backup account does not reduce actual concentration until volume moves. Maintain a dated remediation plan with tested export procedures, alternate receiving capacity, inventory ownership records, and estimated switching cash. Do not create four nominal suppliers controlled by the same parent and call the risk diversified. Aggregate related counterparties and shared failure points. Expansion from five to seven people requires both service pressure and durable contribution coverage after additional loaded cost. Adding seats because gross sales rose can lock the business into a larger payroll just as advertising inflation or supplier withdrawal erases the margin supporting it.

sections.heading: 3. Reconcile canonical earnings to accrual books and transferable rights
paragraphs: Anchor every plan to the canonical scorecard before discussing optimization. Conservative recognized retail revenue is $250,000 at 5%, producing $12,500 annual owner net profit and $237,500 total modeled costs. Base is $1,125,000 at 11.5%, producing $129,375 profit and $995,625 costs. Scaled is $2,000,000 at 18%, producing $360,000 profit and $1,640,000 costs. All three revenue figures represent retail sales net of refunds, despite the scorecard's gross revenue label; they are not marketplace GMV, advertising budgets, or payment-processor deposits. Goods, fulfillment, and advertising already sit inside the margin calculation. The stated $4,000 to $25,000 monthly opex range cannot substitute for the complete cost envelope, which also includes inventory economics and other costs represented in those margins. Build a detailed bridge rather than assuming that range funds every operating requirement. Annual profit divided by twelve gives average monthly earnings of $1,041.67, $10,781.25, and $30,000 respectively, not a promise of monthly distributable cash. Seasonal buying, processor reserves, taxes, and debt service can absorb cash before distributions. The Conservative case is especially fragile for five seats; identify founder labor and fractional contractor capacity explicitly instead of implying that $12,500 comfortably supports additional unbudgeted compensation.

Close monthly on an accrual basis with transaction-level links among Shopify, processor settlements, warehouse movements, purchasing records, and QuickBooks Online or Xero. Establish the revenue-recognition point from the actual customer contract and shipping terms, then apply it consistently. Record inventory purchases as inventory until sold or otherwise expensed; processor payout timing does not determine revenue. Capitalize appropriate freight and duties into landed inventory cost, then release cost through a consistent costing method. Record collected sales tax as a liability where the seller is responsible, and reconcile marketplace-facilitator collections separately. Maintain reserves or estimates for expected returns, damaged goods, chargebacks, and obsolete inventory under the chosen accounting policy, with supporting history and subsequent true-ups. Cohort reports should group customers by first purchase month and channel, then measure realized contribution through a defined observation window. Do not compare a mature twelve-month cohort with a newly acquired thirty-day cohort and call the difference deteriorating retention. Klaviyo attribution is a marketing view, not independent evidence of incremental earnings. Reconcile its claimed sales to actual orders and use holdouts where feasible. Preserve source exports and versioned calculation logic so another operator can reproduce the reported margins without the founder's spreadsheet memory.

Build the transferability file while relationships are healthy. Obtain signed copyright assignments from creative and integration contractors covering the identified deliverables; 17 U.S.C. section 204(a) generally requires a signed writing for copyright ownership transfers. Payment alone does not establish ownership, and a broad work-for-hire label does not solve every contractor arrangement. Separate newly assigned work from licensed fonts, stock photography, open-source components, and preexisting contractor tools, documenting the buyer's continuing usage rights. Store dealer authorizations, territory restrictions, channel permissions, assignment provisions, and change-of-control terms alongside each supplier account. A profitable listing loses value if the buyer cannot continue selling it. Maintain product traceability, supplier certificates where applicable, insurance schedules, incident logs, and recall procedures. Evaluate reporting duties under 15 U.S.C. section 2064(b) when information reasonably supports a reportable product hazard; do not wait for ordinary customer-support thresholds. For imported goods, document who is importer of record and preserve classification, valuation, and duty evidence supporting reasonable care under 19 U.S.C. section 1484. Inventory every privileged account and service credential by business owner, renewal date, and transfer procedure. Transferable books combine reproducible earnings with enforceable operating rights, not merely a tidy income statement.

sections.heading: 4. Underwrite an exit multiple against transferable earnings and cash
paragraphs: Value the business from a defined earnings base, not from the largest revenue number on a broker slide. For a small owner-operated retailer, an illustrative screening range of two to four times normalized annual seller's discretionary earnings can frame discussion; it is a modeling assumption, not a verified transaction-comparable range. Establish current comparables and buyer financing constraints before quoting an asking price. SDE commonly adds back one working owner's compensation and documented discretionary or nonrecurring items, while an absentee buyer must price the replacement labor required to operate the business. Canonical owner net profit is neither automatically SDE nor EBITDA. Reconcile interest, taxes, depreciation, owner compensation, and recurring operating costs before selecting the metric. Advertising required to sustain sales, recurring integration repairs, and ordinary product testing are not discretionary merely because the seller dislikes paying for them. A premium requires repeatable contribution, low unresolved concentration, transferable dealer rights, clean inventory, and evidence that the pod operates without founder rescue. Buyers may discount businesses with heavy marketplace dependence even when revenue is growing. Present trailing monthly earnings and cohort evidence alongside the latest annual total so seasonality and recent margin erosion remain visible throughout underwriting.

Keep illustrative arithmetic separate from the canonical operating cases. Multiplying Base owner profit of $129,375 by two and four produces $258,750 and $517,500; multiplying Scaled profit of $360,000 produces $720,000 and $1,440,000. Those are mechanical earnings-proxy values, not concluded enterprise values, because normalization and deal terms remain unresolved. The same exercise produces only $25,000 to $50,000 for Conservative profit of $12,500, which can be overwhelmed by transaction costs or replacement labor. Suppose a buyer identifies $60,000 of recurring replacement labor absent from Base expenses. Transferable annual earnings would fall to $69,375, and a three-times illustration becomes $208,125. A separate Scaled example with $90,000 of missing recurring replacement cost yields $270,000 and $810,000 at three times. Apply those deductions only when the costs are actually absent; subtracting already included payroll would distort valuation. Neither sensitivity changes the published scorecard. Bridge enterprise value to seller proceeds through debt, cash treatment, transaction expenses, working-capital adjustments, holdbacks, and contingent consideration. Define whether saleable inventory is included in normalized working capital or purchased separately. Counting inventory in both places manufactures proceeds that the purchase agreement will not deliver.

Run a ninety-day transferability rehearsal before seeking offers. During the first month, complete the rights register, reconcile inventory, document contractor capacity, and close unresolved supplier permissions. During the second, have backups perform the weekly review and monthly close while the founder handles only documented escalations. During the third, operate a planned absence period and measure service, contribution, and exception aging against the prior baseline. Record failures honestly and repair the procedures rather than editing the evidence pack. Give prospective buyers staged, access-controlled financial and operational evidence; minimize customer data and follow applicable privacy obligations when preparing diligence exports. Provide aggregate cohort reporting before identifiable records are genuinely required. Keep the cash-cow alternative equally rigorous: fund replenishment, tax liabilities, expected returns, debt commitments, and a measured operating reserve before owner distributions. A reserve based on supplier lead times and downside contribution is more useful than an arbitrary percentage of revenue. Revisit whether the additional scaled seats still protect enough contribution to justify their loaded cost. The best exit preparation also improves continued ownership because each documented right, reconciled balance, and independently executed play reduces the founder's dependence on constant intervention without pretending retail risk has disappeared.

action_checklist: Assign P01 through P18 to the five-seat core, name a trained backup for every play, and document the exact FT3 and C4 transfers before expanding.

chapters.title: The First 30-Day Launch Sprint & Kill / Fix / Scale Gates
chapters.subtitle: A Five-Person Shopify and 3PL Sprint: Contribution Underwriting, Dealer Authorization, FTC Shipping Rules, and Evidence-Based Capital Release
chapters.executive_summary: Candidate #28, Automated E-Commerce, ranks #21 with a 70/100 Money-to-Manpower Score. This sprint turns 18 mapped plays into an accountable launch system for two full-time operators and three contractors. Days 1–30 establish authorized supply, landed economics, tested fulfillment, measured acquisition, and automated retention; they do not compress the stated two-to-six-month first-deal horizon into a sales promise. Use a $35,000 first-month cash ceiling only against $60,000 of committed funding, then release further capital against mature contribution and service evidence. Canonical annual owner profits remain $12,500 Conservative, $129,375 Base, and $360,000 Scaled. Day 30/60/90 decisions separate weak economics from insufficient evidence, with explicit stop conditions for unsafe products, unauthorized supply, and uncontrolled cash exposure.

sections.heading: 1. Days 1–7: Underwrite the Assortment Before Committing Inventory
paragraphs: Day 1 establishes the operating boundary: one domestic market, one storefront, one contracted 3PL, and three to five initial SKUs from authorized suppliers. Candidate #28 has 18 mapped plays; use the following chapter-local execution labels to make that coverage actionable without treating them as separate businesses. P01 selects the niche; P02 verifies dealer authorization; P03 checks product safety; P04 calculates landed cost; P05 underwrites contribution; P06 builds product pages; P07 configures checkout and tax; P08 integrates the 3PL; P09 routes orders; P10 monitors inventory; P11 handles delivery exceptions; P12 tracks returns; P13 tests paid acquisition; P14 captures permissioned email; P15 runs retention; P16 reconciles settlements; P17 controls cash; and P18 makes portfolio decisions. Assign the commercial lead P01–P07, P13, P17, and P18, and the operations lead P08–P12, P14–P16. These are the two full-time seats. Three contractors provide storefront and tracking implementation, creative and lifecycle production, and bookkeeping with tax coordination. The 3PL is a contracted service, not an invisible internal employee. Keep one shared exception queue so contractor handoffs cannot become orphaned work. Record a primary owner and backup for every play before accepting supplier terms.

Days 2–4 turn supplier enthusiasm into documentary evidence. Obtain a signed authorization identifying permitted channels, territories, warranty handling, image rights, and termination terms; a distributor invoice alone does not establish every resale permission. Match product identifiers to applicable test reports and certificates under 15 U.S.C. 2063 and 16 CFR Part 1110 where certification is required. Avoid children's products, ingestibles, batteries, and medical claims in this initial assortment unless the team already has category-specific expertise and documentation. Record lot identifiers and a recall contact, and establish how the operator will assess reporting duties under 15 U.S.C. 2064(b). For imports, identify the importer of record, classification, origin, customs value, duties, and broker before approving landed cost; 19 U.S.C. 1484 places entry responsibilities on the importer. Confirm insurance coverage against the actual category, rather than assuming a general policy covers every product. On Day 4, obtain a written 3PL rate card covering receiving, storage, pick fees, packaging, dimensional weight, returns, and minimum charges. Model the most expensive common shipping zone, not merely the warehouse's neighboring ZIP codes. Reject suppliers whose lead times or evidence cannot support the published customer promise.

Days 5–7 establish a cash envelope before placing the opening purchase order. This illustrative sprint requires $60,000 of committed funding, within the candidate's $30,000–$250,000 startup range, and caps first-month cash commitments at $35,000: $16,000 inventory and inbound freight, $12,000 loaded payroll and contractor work, $3,000 advertising, $2,000 systems and setup, and $2,000 contingency. The noninventory envelope is therefore $19,000, inside the stated $4,000–$25,000 monthly operating range, although actual accounting classification follows the underlying expense. Keep the remaining $25,000 uncommitted; customer receipts do not automatically enlarge spending authority. Inventory purchases consume cash immediately but become cost of goods as units sell, subject to impairment. Obtain real staffing quotes: the labor allowance is an assumption, not evidence that every market can supply five people at that cost. If loaded staffing exceeds it, revise funding and scope before purchase, rather than hiding unpaid owner labor inside profit. Stage the inventory commitment with the supplier and include cancellation exposure in the cash ledger. An operator starting with only $30,000 should complete validation and negotiate smaller orders instead of attempting this entire funded configuration.

sections.heading: 2. Days 8–14: Prove Checkout, Routing, and Exception Recovery
paragraphs: Days 8–10 build a narrow transaction path rather than a decorative storefront. Use Shopify for catalog and checkout, the contracted 3PL's supported connector for fulfillment, and QuickBooks Online or Xero for the accounting destination; select one accounting system, not both. The implementation contractor creates a staging checklist while the commercial lead owns prices, product claims, shipping promises, and customer-facing policies. For every SKU, publish dimensions, compatibility limits, warranty route, and realistic dispatch timing. Under 16 CFR Part 435, maintain a reasonable basis for the stated shipping time; if shipment cannot occur as promised, follow the applicable delay-notice, cancellation, consent, and refund requirements. Do not let a template promise same-day shipment when the warehouse cutoff makes that impossible. P07 includes determining registration obligations from physical presence, inventory location, and each destination state's economic nexus rules. A tax calculation app does not perform every registration or filing duty. The bookkeeping contractor produces a jurisdiction worksheet and the commercial lead resolves required registrations before affected sales begin. Restrict collection of customer data to operational needs, configure role-based access, and document the privacy requests workflow applicable to the actual business.

Days 11–12 attack the integration's failure paths. Send one normal order, one duplicate event, one cancellation, one partial allocation, one address correction, and one refund through controlled tests. Shopify webhooks may arrive more than once; use the order identifier and fulfillment operation as an idempotency key so a retry cannot create a second shipment. Authenticate incoming events, minimize stored customer fields, and place failed messages into a visible retry queue with an assigned owner. Distinguish financial authorization, capture, warehouse acceptance, label creation, carrier acceptance, and delivery. A purchased label is not proof that the parcel entered the carrier network. The operations lead reconciles available inventory against allocated orders and warehouse counts twice daily during launch. Set the reorder point from expected daily demand multiplied by replenishment lead time, then add explicit safety stock; for two units daily, fourteen days of lead time, and ten buffer units, the alert triggers at thirty-eight units. Keep safety stock separate from sellable stock when publishing availability. Never enable uncontrolled backorders to conceal a connector delay. Record each test's expected state, observed state, timestamp, and recovery owner so another person can reproduce the result.

Days 13–14 prove the customer and accounting loops before paid traffic arrives. The operations lead creates return reason codes, photographs condition standards, and defines who decides restock, refurbish, supplier credit, or disposal. P12 must connect a return authorization to the original order, physical receipt, refund, and inventory adjustment; an email thread alone is not a returns ledger. Configure Klaviyo or an equivalent lifecycle system for separately identified transactional and commercial messages. Under 15 U.S.C. 7704, commercial email needs accurate routing information, appropriate identification, a valid postal address, and a functioning opt-out honored within the statutory period. Suppress unsubscribed recipients from promotional flows while retaining necessary order service communications with correctly limited content. The creative contractor prepares first-purchase education and replenishment messages only where product usage supports them. The bookkeeping contractor then reconciles three controlled orders across storefront, payment processor, warehouse, and accounting records, including fees and one refund. Require zero unexplained order-level differences before publishing acquisition campaigns. Test orders remain excluded from customer conversion and contribution reports. Finish the week with a recorded handoff showing how either full-time operator can pause ads, disable a SKU, and locate a delayed shipment.

sections.heading: 3. Days 15–21: Buy Measured Evidence Without Buying Uncontrolled Losses
paragraphs: Days 15–17 release a small acquisition experiment only after stock is available and acceptance tests pass. The commercial lead selects one paid channel, either Google Shopping for existing search demand or Meta for demonstrable visual differentiation, rather than splitting a small budget across both. Start at $100 daily for three days, with the full sprint's paid-media commitment capped at $3,000. The creative contractor supplies two materially different messages for the same qualified audience and landing page; changing audience, offer, and page simultaneously makes diagnosis ambiguous. Tag campaigns consistently and join acquisition source to order identifiers in the storefront export. Platform-reported return on ad spend remains a diagnostic, not recognized revenue or profit. Reconcile attributed purchases against paid customer orders and separate existing customers from new customers. Calculate acquisition cost as channel spend divided by attributable new customers, reporting attribution limitations explicitly. If there are no customers, report spend and zero conversions rather than fabricating a cost ratio. Pause a creative after $150 without a purchase, inspect the funnel, and resume only with a documented correction. This is a spend-control rule, not statistical proof that the product cannot sell.

Day 18 replaces attractive dashboard ratios with order-level contribution. In the illustrative unit model, $110 of merchandise charges less $10 of expected refunds produces $100 of net retail sales, excluding sales tax. Subtract $40 landed product cost, $12 outbound fulfillment and shipping, $3 payment fees, and $3 return handling to produce $42 of contribution before acquisition, called CM1. Subtract $25 acquisition cost to produce $17 CM2, or 17% of net sales. Return handling is a separate expense, not a second deduction of the refunded selling price. Replace estimates with actual cohort results as returns mature, including inventory recovery and nonrecoverable fees. CM2 still excludes fixed payroll, software, insurance, and other overhead; it is not owner profit. At the canonical Base revenue of $1,125,000, a hypothetical 17% blended CM2 would yield $191,250 before fixed expenses. Reaching the canonical $129,375 owner profit would then leave only $61,875 for those expenses, a tight constraint that must be tested against actual staffing. If fixed costs exceed it, the model needs better blended contribution, not relabeling of payroll. The Scaled 18% net margin likewise requires contribution above 18% whenever fixed costs remain positive.

Days 19–21 test whether automation reduces work without concealing service debt. Inspect every late dispatch, stock discrepancy, refund request, and delivery exception daily. Measure dispatch performance against the published promise using orders whose dispatch deadline has elapsed; exclude neither difficult destinations nor cancelled warehouse mistakes merely to improve the rate. Track order accuracy from verified picks and customer reports, and keep the denominator visible. P15 can test post-purchase education and a relevant accessory offer, but projected repeat purchases never rescue a losing first-order acquisition case. Measure repeat contribution only after the repeat order settles and its return exposure is provisioned. Limit the launch queue to five open noncritical exceptions per full-time operator and require an initial response within one business day. If unresolved work exceeds that capacity for two consecutive days, pause acquisition expansion and repair the dominant failure. Stop paid traffic immediately when cumulative observed CM2 loss, including refund provisions, reaches $750. This acquisition-loss limit sits inside, not above, the $3,000 media envelope. Neither limit replaces the $35,000 total cash ceiling, and favorable processor settlements do not authorize automatic replenishment spending.

callout.title: Four Ways Experienced Operators Preserve the Experiment
callout.body: Protect the quality of the evidence before trying to improve the reported conversion rate.
items: Ask the 3PL for parcel-level billed dimensions; one oversized carton can destroy the margin that an average shipping quote suggests.
Keep a separate SKU ledger for returns awaiting inspection so damaged goods cannot silently reappear as available inventory.
Use an order-level acquisition export alongside platform attribution; duplicate purchase events often look like sudden marketing improvement.
Negotiate staged supplier releases with written cancellation terms before seeking a lower unit price tied to an oversized opening order.

sections.heading: 4. Days 22–30 and Day 60/90: Separate Kill, Fix, and Scale Decisions
paragraphs: Days 22–30 turn the launch into a repeatable decision packet. A mature order has passed the disclosed return window plus seven days, with a minimum observation period of thirty days after delivery; maintain additional reserves for later disputes and warranty exposure. The thresholds below are operating choices for this experiment, not scorecard forecasts. A fresh store will usually lack mature orders on Day 30, and the candidate's two-to-six-month first-deal horizon makes a pre-revenue checkpoint entirely plausible. Classify that condition as Fix: continue bounded validation or wait for evidence, without calling missing data product failure. For each checkpoint, examine the latest ninety days of mature orders and require at least 100 at Day 30, 200 at Day 60, or 300 at Day 90 before granting Scale. Require at least fifty mature orders within any SKU and acquisition segment proposed for expansion. Pool only operationally comparable orders, and disclose concentration in a single product or campaign. These counts are minimum evidence floors, not statistical certainty. Add a stress calculation with acquisition cost increased 20% and net sales reduced 5%, holding other unit costs constant; stressed CM2 must remain positive.

Apply decisions in a fixed precedence order. First, Kill means stop the affected SKU, supplier, campaign, or automation path immediately for missing required safety evidence, revoked authorization, an unresolved serious safety signal, or a committed-cash breach. Assess reporting and customer remediation separately; stopping ads does not resolve an existing product hazard. Next, once the evidence floor is met, kill an economic test when mature CM2 is zero or negative after two documented corrective experiments, each observed through cohort maturity. Before those experiments mature, Fix applies and spending remains paused or separately bounded. Scale requires mature CM2 of at least 8%, 12%, and 15% at Days 30, 60, and 90 respectively, on-time dispatch of at least 98%, verified order accuracy of at least 99%, unit return rate no greater than 8%, and positive stressed CM2. Use the same mature cohort for return rates and contribution; report counts beside percentages. All other outcomes are Fix with one owner, one specific hypothesis, and a seven-day implementation deadline. Reaching that deadline proves execution only; it does not accelerate the return window. Stop the whole venture only when the constraint is systemic or remaining capital cannot fund a credible bounded repair.

Scale releases controlled increments, not a new annual revenue claim. Require unrestricted cash to cover at least ninety days of committed fixed cash costs plus separately reserved taxes, refunds, and supplier payables. This reserve test is stricter than the initial $25,000 buffer and may block expansion until additional funding or retained contribution exists. With all tests passed, increase paid spend no more than 20% per seven days and order no more than six weeks of forecast demand, adjusted for actual lead time. Obtain a new dated cash budget for Days 31–60 and 61–90; the original sprint ceiling never silently renews. Keep the two-full-time, three-contractor pod until sustained workload and contribution fund another seat. The canonical Scaled configuration is three full-time people plus four contractors, seven people total, not an unsupported five-person staffing promise. Preserve the annual scorecard exactly: $250,000 net-of-refund retail revenue at 5% produces $12,500 owner profit; $1,125,000 at 11.5% produces $129,375; $2,000,000 at 18% produces $360,000. These are complete annual scenarios after goods, fulfillment, advertising, and operating costs, not thirty-day run rates. Archive the Day 30 packet with signed decisions, evidence links, unresolved assumptions, and the next checkpoint date.

chapters.pull_quote: Automate the repeatable transaction, measure the expensive exception, and scale only the contribution that survives both.
action_checklist: Assign all eighteen execution plays across two full-time owners and three scoped contractors, with a backup owner for every exception queue.
Complete SKU-level authorization, applicable safety evidence, landed-cost underwriting, and staged purchase terms before releasing inventory funds.
Fund the illustrative $60,000 configuration, enforce the $35,000 first-month commitment ceiling, and preserve the separate $25,000 initial reserve.
Pass checkout, duplicate-event, cancellation, inventory, return, email-suppression, and settlement tests before enabling paid acquisition.
Report mature CM2 separately from owner profit, enforce the $3,000 media ceiling and $750 contribution-loss stop, and retain order-level evidence.
Sign Day 30/60/90 Kill, Fix, or Scale decisions using maturity floors, service thresholds, downside contribution, and the ninety-day cash-reserve test.
